questions.prompt: The Law of Sines states:
questions.explanation: Each side divided by the sine of its OPPOSITE angle gives the same value.

questions.prompt: Which case can the Law of Sines solve?
questions.explanation: You need a complete side–opposite-angle pair, which AAS (and ASA and SSA) provides. SAS and SSS need the Law of Cosines.

questions.prompt: Which case CANNOT be started with the Law of Sines?
questions.explanation: With three sides and no angles there is no complete pair to work from.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 40^\circ$, $m\angle B = 75^\circ$ and $a = 10$. Find $b$. (Nearest tenth.)
questions.explanation: $b = \dfrac{a\sin B}{\sin A} = \dfrac{10\sin 75^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} \approx 15.0$.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 40^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 75^\circ$. Find $m\angle C$.
questions.explanation: $180^\circ - 40^\circ - 75^\circ = 65^\circ$ — always find the third angle first in an ASA/AAS problem.

questions.prompt: In an ASA problem, what should you do before applying the Law of Sines?
questions.explanation: ASA gives no complete side–angle pair until you know the angle opposite the given side.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 12$, $m\angle A = 50^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 60^\circ$. Which sets up $b$ correctly?
questions.explanation: Every side pairs with the sine of the angle OPPOSITE it.

questions.prompt: The 'ambiguous case' of the Law of Sines refers to:
questions.explanation: Two sides and a NON-included angle may fit zero, one or two different triangles.

questions.prompt: In the SSA case with $a = 8$, $b = 12$ and $m\angle A = 30^\circ$, what is $\sin B$?
questions.explanation: $\sin B = \dfrac{b\sin A}{a} = \dfrac{12(0.5)}{8} = 0.75$.

questions.prompt: Continuing that case, how many triangles are possible?
questions.explanation: $\sin B = 0.75$ gives $B \approx 48.6^\circ$ or $131.4^\circ$, and both keep the angle sum under $180^\circ$ — so two triangles exist.

questions.prompt: In an SSA case you compute $\sin B = 1.54$. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: Sine can never exceed $1$, so those measurements cannot close into a triangle.

questions.prompt: In an SSA case you compute $\sin B = 1$. How many triangles exist?
questions.explanation: $B = 90^\circ$ is the only possibility, giving a single right triangle.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $b = 9$, $m\angle B = 45^\circ$ and $m\angle C = 60^\circ$. Find $c$. (Nearest tenth.)
questions.explanation: $c = \dfrac{9\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} \approx \dfrac{9(0.866)}{0.707} \approx 11.0$.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 14$, $b = 10$ and $m\angle A = 65^\circ$. Find $m\angle B$ to the nearest degree.
questions.explanation: $\sin B = \dfrac{10\sin 65^\circ}{14} \approx 0.647$, so $B \approx 40^\circ$. (The obtuse option $140^\circ$ is impossible: $65^\circ + 140^\circ > 180^\circ$.)

questions.prompt: When the given angle is obtuse in an SSA problem, how many triangles are possible at most?
questions.explanation: A triangle can only have one obtuse angle, so the second (obtuse) solution is ruled out.

questions.prompt: Why is $\sin^{-1}$ not enough on its own in the SSA case?
choices: a calculator only returns the acute angle, but the obtuse supplement may also work
the Law of Sines is only for right triangles
you must always use cosine instead
questions.explanation: $\sin \theta = \sin(180^\circ - \theta)$, so you must consider the supplement and test whether it fits.

questions.prompt: A triangle has $m\angle A = 100^\circ$, $m\angle B = 30^\circ$ and $a = 20$. Find $b$. (Nearest tenth.)
questions.explanation: $b = \dfrac{20\sin 30^\circ}{\sin 100^\circ} \approx \dfrac{10}{0.985} \approx 10.2$.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct rearrangement of the Law of Sines to find an ANGLE?
questions.explanation: Cross-multiply $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$ and solve for $\sin B$.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 35^\circ$, $a = 5$ and $b = 12$. How many triangles are possible?
questions.explanation: $\sin B = \dfrac{12\sin 35^\circ}{5} \approx 1.38 > 1$, which is impossible — no triangle.

questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are $50^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, and the side between them is $10$. Which law starts this problem?
choices: the Law of Sines, after finding the third angle
questions.explanation: This is ASA — find the third angle ($70^\circ$), then the Law of Sines gives every side.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = 20$ and $m\angle B = 30^\circ$. Find $b$.
questions.explanation: All three ratios are equal, so $b = 20\sin 30^\circ = 10$.

questions.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 70^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 55^\circ$. What is $m\angle C$, in degrees?
questions.explanation: $180^\circ - 70^\circ - 55^\circ = 55^\circ$.
